cat_7.name: State or Status Changes Not Programmatically Exposed

examples.issue_summary: After adding an item to the cart, the "Add to Bag" button visually changes to a checkmark indicating success, but this state change is not announced to screen readers or exposed programmatically.

evidence.verification: Using a screen reader, navigate to a product page, select a size, and activate the "Add to Bag" button. The button visually updates to a checkmark, but no status message or announcement indicates that the item was added to the cart.

examples.notes: Observed by navigating to a product page, selecting an item size, and activating the "Add to Bag" button. The confirmation of the action is conveyed only through a visual change (checkmark) with no accompanying screen reader announcement or aria-live status message.

examples.element: Plan selection tabs (Performance, Security, Reliability, Serverless)
examples.issue_summary: Activating plan selection controls updates the visible content on the page, but the change in state and content is not announced to screen readers or programmatically conveyed.

evidence.verification: With a screen reader enabled, navigate to the plan selection controls and activate different plan options. The screen reader announces only the focused button and does not indicate that the displayed plan content has changed.

examples.notes: The plan options function as tab-like controls that dynamically update in-page content. No status message, selection state, or focus movement communicates the content change to assistive technologies.

examples.element: 'Name' input field and global validation error banner
examples.issue_summary: A form validation error is displayed visually at the top of the page, but the text is not programmatically associated with the specific input field that caused the error.

evidence.dom_snippet: <input placeholder="Type here..." name="_systemfield_name" required="" id="_systemfield_name" type="text" class="..." value="">
evidence.verification: Inspected the 'Name' input field after triggering a validation error. The red error banner ('Missing entry for required field: Name') appears visually, but the input element lacks an 'aria-describedby' or 'aria-errormessage' attribute linking it to the error text's ID. A screen reader focused on the input will not announce the specific error.

examples.notes: Crucial ABD failure for form interaction. Sighted users can visually map the global error banner to the specific field, but assistive technologies require explicit programmatic association to provide context during correction.

examples.issue_summary: The confirmation of a successful 'Add to Bag' action is entirely silent to assistive technologies. The injected DOM lacks any ARIA live region or status role, and the temporary nature of the element (5-second timeout) prevents manual discovery via touch or tab navigation.

evidence.verification: Used the F8 Pause trick to capture the transient DOM. Verified the absence of role='status', role='alert', or aria-live on the parent container. Observed that VoiceOver/NVDA do not announce the item details upon injection.
evidence.html_snapshot: html_snapshots/cat_7/Men’s Dark beige Jacket with Collar _ H&M US.htm

examples.notes: Classic, 'Invisible State Change.' The developer used semantic <dl> tags but forgot the delivery mechanism (aria-live), making the confirmation visual-only.

examples.issue_summary: Unstoppable looping video (General SC 2.2.2 Failure). The promo video is set to `autoplay` and `loop` infinitely. While it avoids F93 (SC 1.4.2) by correctly using the `muted` attribute, it completely fails SC 2.2.2 (Pause, Stop, Hide). The video plays for longer than 5 seconds and is presented in parallel with other content, yet the developer omitted the native `controls` attribute and provided no custom mechanism to pause or stop the motion.

evidence.dom_snippet:
<video autoplay="" loop="" muted="" playsinline="">
  <source src="doomlingopromo2.mp4" type="video/mp4">
  Your browser doesn't support video playback.
</video>
evidence.verification: Inspected the <video> element. Verified it plays automatically on load and loops continuously. Confirmed the presence of the 'muted' attribute (bypassing 1.4.2). Searched the DOM for a native 'controls' attribute or an adjacent pause/stop mechanism and found neither, confirming a 2.2.2 motion failure.

examples.notes: An excellent example of 'silent but inaccessible' media. Developers frequently mute background videos to bypass browser autoplay restrictions and SC 1.4.2 audio rules, but fail to realize that the persistent visual motion still strictly requires a pause mechanism under SC 2.2.2.

examples.element: Global desktop layout (Header, navigation, and product grids)
examples.issue_summary: The desktop site relies on User-Agent sniffing rather than responsive CSS media queries. At 400% zoom (320px viewport), the layout does not reflow into a single column, forcing users to scroll horizontally to read product titles and access the search bar.

evidence.verification: Zoomed the desktop browser to 400%. The global header, search bar, and product carousels remained in a fixed, wide layout. A horizontal scrollbar appeared at the bottom of the viewport, requiring two-dimensional scrolling to read a single sentence of product descriptions.

examples.notes: A prime example of how serving distinct mobile/desktop sites based on device type (rather than viewport width) severely alienates low-vision desktop users who rely on screen magnification.

examples.element: Global header, navigation, and product grid layouts
examples.issue_summary: At 400% zoom (320px viewport), the layout does not reflow into a single column. The rigid desktop layout persists, forcing users into two-dimensional (horizontal and vertical) scrolling to view products and read text.

evidence.verification: Zoomed the desktop browser to 400%. The global header and main product grids failed to stack vertically. A persistent horizontal scrollbar appeared, requiring the user to scroll right just to see the end of a product name or access the shopping bag icon.

examples.notes: Classic F110 failure. The site relies on a separate mobile domain or strict user-agent sniffing rather than responsive CSS breakpoints, breaking the experience for desktop screen magnifier users.

examples.element: Homepage news grid and top navigation bar
examples.issue_summary: The viewport fails to reflow content into a single column when zoomed to 400%. Users must scroll horizontally to read full article headlines and access the top navigation menu.

evidence.verification: Applied 400% browser zoom to simulate a 320px width. The article cards and top navigation did not collapse into a single-column mobile view. Reading a standard headline required scrolling horizontally back and forth across the page.

examples.notes: Severe ABD failure for a global news platform. Low-vision users are forced to track text across two dimensions, drastically increasing cognitive load and reading time.

examples.issue_summary: The mega-menu that appears on hover is not dismissible without moving the pointer. Pressing the Escape key does not close the menu, trapping keyboard and screen-magnifier users.

evidence.verification: Hovered the mouse pointer over the 'Categories' button, which triggered a massive dropdown menu obscuring the page content. Without moving the mouse, pressed the 'Escape' key. The menu remained open, failing the 1.4.13 'Dismissible' requirement.

examples.notes: The develofindeper attached mouseenter/mouseleave events but failed to attach a global keydown listener for the Escape key to allow users to quickly clear their viewport.

examples.element: Fund Flows bar chart data tooltip
examples.issue_summary: The informational tooltip triggered by hovering over a chart bar is not hoverable. The popup disappears immediately when the user attempts to move their pointer from the trigger element to the tooltip itself.

evidence.verification: Navigated from Landing page to ETF Screener, then to VOO ETF, then to the Fund Flows chart and hovered over a specific bar to trigger the data tooltip. Carefully attempted to move the mouse cursor from the SVG bar directly into the HTML tooltip overlay. The tooltip vanished the millisecond the cursor left the bar's bounding box, failing the 'Hoverable' requirement.

examples.notes: Because the tooltip's hit area does not safely overlap or connect with the trigger's hit area, users cannot interact with or magnify the tooltip content.

cat_9.name: Meaningful Sequence and Reading Order Failures

examples.issue_summary: Required fields are indicated only by an asterisk (*) without any textual explanation or instruction defining the meaning of the symbol.

evidence.verification: On the application form, multiple input fields include an asterisk next to their labels, but no instruction or legend on the page explains that the asterisk denotes a required field.

examples.notes: The form relies on a visual convention (asterisk) to indicate required inputs without providing explicit instructions such as "Fields marked with * are required." This can create ambiguity for users who are unfamiliar with the convention or who rely on assistive technologies.

examples.element: Sign up / Confirm it's you email input field
examples.issue_summary: The email input field relies solely on placeholder text to convey that an email address is required, and this instruction disappears once the user begins typing.

evidence.verification: On the BuzzFeed sign-up flow, the email input field initially displays the placeholder text "Enter your email." Once the user starts typing, the placeholder disappears and there is no persistent visible label or instruction indicating that the field requires an email address.

examples.notes: Using placeholder text as the only means of conveying input instructions violates WCAG guidance, as the instruction is not persistent. Users who pause, return focus to the field, or rely on cognitive or memory support may lose context about what information is required.

examples.element: Sign-in form input field and 'Continue' button
examples.issue_summary: When an invalid input is detected, the system silently disables the 'Continue' submission button. It fails to provide any text-based error message explaining why the input is invalid or why the user is blocked from proceeding.

evidence.verification: Entered a single random character into the sign-in field. The system automatically disabled the 'Continue' button to prevent submission, indicating it detected an input error. However, no error text (e.g., 'Please enter a valid email address') was provided to the user, leaving screen reader and cognitive-impaired users without guidance.

examples.notes: A severe 3.3.1 and 3.3.3 failure. The system actively detects the formatting error but relies entirely on the disabled state of a button to communicate it, completely failing to identify the error in text or suggest a valid format.

examples.issue_summary: Split date inputs lack a programmatic group label, stripping away context. While individual inputs have aria-labels (Month, Day, Year), they are not wrapped in a <fieldset> with a <legend> (or an equivalent aria-group), meaning screen reader users lose the overarching context of what the date fields refer to.

evidence.dom_snippet: / /
evidence.verification: Inspected the jQuery-generated date input. Verified that while individual text inputs contain aria-labels, there is no parent container utilizing <fieldset>/<legend> or role='group' with aria-labelledby to associate the 'Event Date' context with the isolated inputs.

examples.notes: Navigation: After going to vitalcheck.com, navigate to 'Order Certificate,' then to 'Birth Certificate,' then 'Start Order.' This is a prime example of a JavaScript UI plugin (jQuery DTE) generating visually formatted components that inherently break WCAG structural grouping requirements.

examples.issue_summary: Password requirements are not programmatically associated with the input field (F1 / SC 3.3.2). While a visual instruction ('at least 6 characters') is present below the field, the <input> element lacks an 'aria-describedby' attribute to link to that text. Consequently, screen reader users are not informed of the specific password constraints upon focusing the field, leading to blind trial-and-error entries.

evidence.dom_snippet: Passwords must be at least 6 characters.
evidence.verification: Inspected the registration form DOM. Confirmed the password requirements text is contained in a separate div with no ID-to-ID relationship (aria-describedby) with the password input. Tested with a screen reader; the '6 character' requirement was not announced when the password field gained focus.

examples.notes: Even though the field correctly identifies itself as 'required' via ARIA, it fails to provide the 'how' (the instructions). This is a common F1 variant where information is visually available but structurally 'hidden' from the accessibility tree because it isn't linked to the control.
